pools.title: Runner pools
pools.intro: A pool keeps runners waiting on one of your servers, so a job runs there instead of on GitHub's machines. Each one registers, takes a single job, and disappears - nothing is left on the machine between jobs.
pools.snippet: Once a pool exists, this is what sends a job to it:

On its settings page add Repository permissions > Administration: Read and write for repository runners, or Organization permissions > Self-hosted runners: Read and write for organization-wide ones, then approve the request on each installation.

guide.title: How it works
guide.description: Running GitHub Actions on your own machines: what to set up, what to change in a workflow, and what to be careful with.

connect.title: 1. Connect GitHub, with permission to register runners
connect.body: Polaris registers a runner on your behalf, which needs more than reading a repository. Under Integrations, connect GitHub and give it Administration: read and write on the repositories you want runners for, or Self-hosted runners: read and write on the organization to cover all of them at once.
connect.app: A GitHub App is the better of the two connections: it can hold the narrow organization permission instead of blanket repository administration, its tokens expire on their own, and it does not belong to one person's account.

pool.title: 2. Add a pool
pool.body: A pool is one machine plus the repositories it serves. <link>Add one</link> and pick the server, how many jobs it may take at once, and whether jobs run in a container or in a directory on the machine.
pool.container: Prefer the container. A job in a container is thrown away with it; a job in a directory is a clean slate but not a boundary, and it can reach whatever the Polaris login on that machine can.

workflow.title: 3. Point a workflow at it
workflow.body: Change one line. Where a workflow says runs-on: ubuntu-latest, it now says the labels your pool registered with:
workflow.then: The next run queues on GitHub, Polaris notices, starts a runner for that repository, and the job lands on it. Each runner takes a single job and disappears, so nothing is left behind between jobs.

repos.title: 4. Decide what each repository may run
repos.body: Under <link>Repositories</link> every repository a pool serves has its own settings: which events run here (pushes, pull requests, on a schedule, by hand), whether pull requests from forks run at all, and whether its jobs can read your secrets.
repos.check: The check happens on the machine, after GitHub hands the job over and before any step of it runs, so a job that is not allowed never executes anything. It shows up under <link>Runs</link> as turned down, with the reason - which is what the person waiting on a red check needs.

secrets.title: 5. Give the runners what they need to read
secrets.body: <link>Secrets</link> are values your machines carry into a job: a registry login, an endpoint that only exists inside your network, a key you would rather not upload to GitHub. They arrive as environment variables, so a step reads one as <env></env>.
secrets.github: These are not GitHub's secrets and do not appear in <expression></expression> - only GitHub can fill that in. A secret can apply to every repository a pool serves or to one of them, and the narrower one wins.

careful.title: What to be careful with
careful.public: <lead>Public repositories.</lead> Anybody on GitHub can open a pull request against one, and a pull request can change the workflow that runs. That is why Polaris will not serve a public repository until you say so on that repository, and why GitHub recommends never pointing a self-hosted runner at one.
careful.forks: <lead>Pull requests from forks.</lead> The code in one was written by whoever opened it. They are turned down by default. Turning them on for a repository means strangers' code runs on that machine with whatever the environment holds - which is why the secrets switch sits next to it.
careful.network: <lead>A container is not a promise about the network.</lead> A contained job cannot reach the machine's files, but it can reach whatever that machine can reach on the network. A runner on a box inside your network is inside your network.
careful.budgets: <lead>Budgets are per repository.</lead> A pool shared between repositories can be given a minute budget and a daily job limit so one busy repository is not the only one that ever gets served.

nothing.title: When nothing runs
nothing.card: The pool card says what is wrong with the pool - an unreachable machine, a missing permission, a repository over its budget. A job that reached a runner and was turned down says so under Runs, with the rule that turned it down.
nothing.labels: If the workflow is still queued on GitHub and neither screen says anything, check that its runs-on labels match the pool's exactly - GitHub only offers a job to a runner carrying every label the job asked for.
